title: Set Work Study: Defying Gravity (Schwartz) — Structure, Melody and Harmony
content_html:
Why Defying Gravity Matters in Your Listening Exam

Defying Gravity comes from the area of study Music for Stage and Screen, and it sits alongside John Williams’ Star Wars main title as one of your two set works there. Written by Stephen Schwartz for the musical Wicked, which opened in 2003, the song closes the first act and marks the moment its central character, Elphaba, makes an irreversible personal choice. Examiners love this set work because it packs almost every musical-theatre device — recitative-style dialogue, a memorable pop-rock chorus, dramatic key changes and a soaring vocal climax — into roughly five minutes.

Because it is a stage number rather than absolute music, every musical decision serves the drama. When you answer questions on this set work, always link the musical feature you spot to what it achieves dramatically: a leap upward is not just ‘a wide interval’, it is a musical depiction of triumph, defiance or flight. Examiners reward that connection between musical language and dramatic function highly.

Key facts to fix in memory: composer Stephen Schwartz; from the musical Wicked (2003); sung at the end of Act One by the character Elphaba; blends a Broadway ballad opening with a driving pop-rock chorus and a belted, orchestral final section.

Structure: From Recitative to Soaring Coda

The song unfolds in a loose but purposeful sectional structure typical of the ‘button song’ that ends a musical-theatre act. It opens with a recitative-like passage: free, speech-rhythm vocal lines over sparse, sustained chords, allowing dialogue and internal thought to unfold almost like sung conversation rather than a fixed melody. This recitative section deliberately avoids a strong pulse or repeating pattern, so that when the song’s first real melodic idea does arrive, its regularity feels like a release of tension.

From there the song settles into a verse–chorus core, the most familiar pop-song shape in the set work list. Each verse builds harmonic and rhythmic momentum before arriving at a chorus built on the rising melodic idea discussed below. Unlike a typical three-minute pop song, though, Defying Gravity keeps intensifying: verses shorten, choruses grow, and material that first appeared quietly returns fortissimo.

The song’s final section abandons the verse–chorus alternation altogether. Material from the chorus returns transformed — higher, louder, doubled by full orchestra and (in the stage production) chorus voices — before a held, extended final note functions as the coda. This coda is the moment examiners most often quote in listening extracts, since its combination of sustained top note, thick orchestral texture and maximum dynamic makes it instantly identifiable.

Structure to remember: free recitative-style opening → verse–chorus core with intensifying repeats → extended, transformed final section → sustained climactic coda.

Melody: The Rising Motif and Pentatonic Colour

The song’s most quoted melodic idea is a short, rising figure first heard under the word most associated with the song’s theme of freedom — sometimes nicknamed the ‘unlimited’ motif by analysts because of where it falls in the text. It moves upward by step and small leap, outlining part of a scale before settling briefly, and its rising shape is repeated and extended at each appearance, arriving slightly higher in pitch each time. This is a simple but highly effective device: melodic sequence combined with rising register creates a physical sensation of ascent that mirrors the song’s flying imagery.

Listen to a full performance of the number and track how many times that rising figure returns. Notice, too, how Schwartz colours several phrases with a pentatonic scale — a five-note scale missing the semitone steps of the full major or minor scale. Pentatonic melody has an open, unforced quality, which contrasts effectively with the more chromatic, tension-filled harmony underneath it, so the tune sounds confident and simple even while the accompaniment is doing something harmonically complex.

As the song approaches its coda, the melody stops developing gradually and instead leaps directly to extreme high pitches, wide-leap climaxes that demand a powerful, sustained belt from the singer. These leaps are the clearest musical symbol of ‘defying gravity’ in the whole number: the tune is, quite literally, thrown as high as the voice can safely go, and the register never resolves downward before the song ends.

Harmony and Tonality: Key Changes as Dramatic Lift

Modulation is the harmonic engine of this set work. Rather than staying in one key throughout, the song shifts upward in pitch level more than once, each new key arriving at a moment of heightened emotional stakes. This device, common in musical theatre and often called a ‘lift’ or step-up modulation, has an almost physical effect on a listener: the whole texture seems to rise with the melody, reinforcing the flying, ascending imagery discussed above.

What makes Schwartz’s handling distinctive for exam purposes is that at least one of these shifts is not the expected, closely related move to the dominant or subdominant. Instead the music slips to a key a third away from where it started, changing mode in the process — a chromatic mediant relationship. Because chromatic mediant keys share few or no common chords with the previous key, the modulation feels sudden and slightly magical rather than smoothly logical, which suits the song’s theme of transformation and a character stepping outside the normal rules that bind her.

Harmony checklist: step-up modulations raise tension with each repeat; at least one modulation is a chromatic mediant shift rather than a move to a closely related key; tonality generally trends from minor-tinged uncertainty toward a firm major-key resolution at the climax.

Rhythm, Texture and Orchestration

Underneath the vocal line, the accompaniment is built from a persistent, driving quaver pattern — repeated broken chords or block chords played in continuous quavers by piano, guitar and rhythm-section instruments. This constant quaver motion supplies forward momentum and urgency throughout the verses and choruses.

Against that busy accompaniment, the vocal line frequently uses long, held notes, especially at the ends of phrases and throughout the coda. This contrast between rhythmically active accompaniment and sustained, static vocal pitches is a texture examiners specifically look for: describe it as a held melodic line over a continuous rhythmic ostinato in the accompaniment, and you are using precise vocabulary that scores well.

Orchestration thickens steadily across the song. The recitative opening uses minimal scoring — just enough sustained chords to support the voice. By the final section the full pit orchestra, including strings, brass and woodwind alongside the rock rhythm section, plays together at full dynamic, and in the stage show a chorus of surrounding voices is added too. This gradual thickening of texture and orchestration, moving from sparse to full, is one of the clearest ways the song builds toward its climax, and it is a feature you can compare directly with the build in Beethoven’s Pathétique or the tutti climaxes in the Bach Brandenburg Concerto movement.

Exam Focus: How Questions Target This Set Work

Questions on Defying Gravity typically supply a short audio extract and ask you to identify a feature (a modulation, an interval, an instrument entering) or to explain how a musical device supports the drama or mood. Extracts are commonly drawn from the recitative opening, a verse-to-chorus transition, or the final coda, since these are the moments where features change most clearly and can be tested precisely.

A strong exam answer names the correct musical term and links it to effect: for example, identifying the step-up modulation and explaining that it raises tension and intensifies the character’s resolve, rather than simply stating ‘the key changes’. Similarly, if asked about texture, name both layers — the sustained vocal line and the driving quaver accompaniment — rather than describing texture vaguely as ‘thick’ or ‘busy’.

Finally, remember the comparative value of this set work: because it shares the area of study with a film score, you may be asked to compare how both pieces build tension or climax using orchestration, harmony or dynamics. Revise Defying Gravity’s structural stages and modulation scheme alongside the Star Wars cue so you can draw those comparisons confidently.
exam_tip_html: When a question asks you to "describe the key change" in Defying Gravity, do not just write "it modulates up" — that earns minimal credit. Instead phrase it as: "the music modulates upward to a key a third away with a change of mode (a chromatic mediant relationship), which intensifies the emotional climax because it avoids the expected, smoothly related dominant modulation"; naming the type of modulation and its dramatic function together is what separates a top-band answer from a middle-band one, and this exact error — identifying that a key change happens but not what kind — is the single most common mark loss on this set work.
conclusion_html: You now have the structural map, melodic motifs, modulation scheme and texture of Defying Gravity firmly in place, so revisit the embedded performance a second time and try naming each section, motif entrance and key shift out loud as it plays before moving on to compare it with Music for Stage and Screen's second set work.

practice_questions.text: Identify the term for the free, speech-like vocal section that opens Defying Gravity.
practice_questions.marks: Award 1 mark for the correct term recitative or recitative-style.

practice_questions.text: Describe the melodic device used when the rising motif returns at a higher pitch each time it appears.
practice_questions.marks: Award up to 2 marks for identifying sequence and rising pitch level, with 1 mark for a partial or vague description.

practice_questions.text: Explain how the modulation scheme in Defying Gravity contributes to the song's dramatic build.
practice_questions.marks: Award up to 3 marks for identifying step-up/chromatic mediant modulation and linking it clearly to increasing tension or triumph.

practice_questions.text: Name the scale type used to give some melodic phrases an open, simple quality.
Describe the relationship between the vocal line and the accompaniment texture in the final section of the song.
practice_questions.marks: Award up to 2 marks for identifying sustained/held vocal notes against a continuous rhythmic (quaver/ostinato) accompaniment.

practice_questions.text: Explain how orchestration changes across the song support its dramatic structure, referring to specific sections.
practice_questions.marks: Award up to 4 marks for tracing the shift from sparse recitative scoring to full orchestral and choral texture in the coda, with clear links to increasing dramatic intensity.

knowledge_checks.q: Which musical is Defying Gravity taken from?
What term describes the free, speech-rhythm vocal section at the song's opening?
What kind of scale gives some melodic phrases their open, uncomplicated sound?
What is a chromatic mediant modulation an example of?
options: A move to a key a third away with a mode change
A move to the dominant key
A move by a semitone only

knowledge_checks.q: What texture is heard between the vocal line and accompaniment in the song's climax?
options: Held vocal notes over a driving quaver ostinato
Two equal melodic lines in canon
Call and response between two singers

glossary_terms.definition: A free, speech-like style of vocal writing with flexible rhythm, used to move the drama or dialogue forward.
A short, recognisable musical idea that is repeated and developed throughout a piece.
The repetition of a melodic or harmonic pattern at a higher or lower pitch level.
A five-note scale that omits the semitone steps found in the full major or minor scale, giving an open, simple sound.
The process of changing from one key to another within a piece of music.
A modulation to a key a third away from the original, usually with a change of mode, creating a striking rather than smooth key change.
The organisation of music around a central key, moving between major and minor or between different keys.
A concluding section added to the end of a piece or movement to bring it to a close.
A short musical pattern that is repeated persistently, often in the accompaniment.
The way melodic, harmonic and rhythmic layers are combined in a piece of music.
The way music is arranged and scored for the instruments or voices performing it.
The varying levels of loudness or softness in music.
